headline: Every map lies—projecting a sphere onto a flat surface always distorts something
universal_truth: All representations involve trade-offs; no model perfectly captures reality
fun_facts: Greenland looks as big as Africa on most maps, but Africa is actually 14 times larger
There are hundreds of different map projections, each distorting differently
Some map projections preserve direction, others preserve area—none preserve everything
discussion_questions: What do maps distort that you never noticed?
How might map distortions affect how we see the world?
What other 'maps' of reality do we use that might distort truth?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Look at a world map. Greenland appears huge—almost as big as Africa. But Africa is actually fourteen times larger. Every flat map of our spherical Earth must distort something. The question is: what do you want to get wrong?

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Why can't we make a perfect flat map? What geometric reality makes distortion unavoidable when representing a sphere on a flat surface?
cliff.prompt: Why do all flat maps distort reality?

options.text: A sphere's curved surface can't be flattened without stretching or cutting—like peeling an orange flat
options.response: Yes. Try flattening an orange peel—it tears or stretches. Mapping a sphere to a plane has the same problem.

options.text: Mapmakers make choices about what to emphasize based on their priorities
options.response: Mapmakers do make choices, but the fundamental problem is geometric...

q1.title: The Mercator Problem
q1.script: The Mercator projection, from 1569, preserves direction—crucial for navigation. But it massively distorts size near the poles. Countries like Greenland and Canada appear enormous while equatorial regions shrink. Useful for sailors, misleading for understanding.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "The Mercator Problem"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Impossible Perfection
q2.script: No projection can preserve area, shape, distance, and direction simultaneously. Every map sacrifices some accuracy for others. The choice of projection is a statement about priorities—what matters most for your purpose?
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Mental Maps
q3.script: We carry mental maps shaped by the maps we've seen. If you grew up with Mercator projections, you might unconsciously see wealthy northern countries as larger and more central than they are. Maps shape worldviews.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: All representations involve trade-offs. Maps teach that every model of reality sacrifices something. When you encounter any representation—charts, summaries, explanations—ask: what got distorted to make this?
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 106. Tomorrow, we'll explore how we know which way—navigation. Until then, look at a map and consider what it's distorting.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Map Skepticism - Question Representations
growTrack.learning_objective: Develop awareness of how representations distort reality
growTrack.activity: Look at a world map today—on paper or digitally. Notice how sizes and positions might differ from reality. Then consider: what other 'maps' do you rely on? Charts, graphs, summaries? What might they distort?
